title: NDMA issues flood alert for various parts of country during next 2-3 days
all_text:
(File Photo)
The National Disaster Management Authority has issued a flood alert for various parts of the country during the next two to three days.
According to the NDMA's National Emergencies Operation Center, heavy rainfall accompanied by strong winds and thunderstorms is expected in the upper regions of Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Kashmir and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
The heavy downpour may cause urban flooding, while flooding and landslides are also possible in mountainous terrain.
Flash flood warnings have been issued for vulnerable localities in Gilgit-Baltistan, including Gilgit, Diamer, Ghizer, Hunza, Astore, Skardu and Shigar.
In Azad Kashmir, flood risks persist in sensitive areas including Bagh, Poonch, Muzaffarabad, Haveli, Bhimber, Sudhnoti, Mirpur and Kotli.
Similarly, there is also a risk of flash flooding in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa including Chitral, Dir, Swat, Bajaur, Mohmand, Shangla, Kohistan, Abbottabad and Haripur.
Expected rainfall in Islamabad and Rawalpindi is also likely to cause high water flows in Nullah Lai.
The public is strongly advised to avoid unnecessary movement near glacial rivers, streams and other high-risk locations.
The NDMA has urged citizens to remain updated on weather conditions, early warnings and instructions issued by district administrations, and to utilize the "Pak NDMA Disaster Alert App" for real-time alerts.

title: Joanna Lumley says ‘heartbreaking’ Nepal flood could have been predicted
all_text:
Dame Joanna Lumley has said the “heartbreaking” flash flood in Nepal “could have maybe been predicted” as she attended a vigil to remember those affected by the disaster.
The 80-year-old actress, who has visited Nepal on numerous occasions and has strong ties with the Gurkha community, told the Press Association seeing the flood sweep through the northern part of the country last week “broke her heart”.
Dame Joanna joined members of London’s Nepalese community at a candlelit vigil at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath, south-east London, on Thursday afternoon.
Around fifty people came together at the restaurant to pray for the communities affected by the catastrophe, observe a minute of silence and light candles.
Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday said 1,252 deaths had been recorded since the flash flood on August 26.
It added around 4,200 people remained missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 34 countries.
On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people are currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.
During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: “I think, actually, in this country and around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.
“The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.
“These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn’t something that we haven’t heard of and thought of before.
“When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers.”
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and China.
It added that a “glacial collapse and debris flow” caused “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream”.
Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.
Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, “it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around”.
“It seems that we have been warned about this over the years,” she added.
“Now, there are two camps, as we both know: there is the people who believe that climate change is largely affected by mankind and those who just say that it’s completely a natural phenomenon.
“I belong to the first camp, which is that I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.
“And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there.”
Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.
Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.
Also present at the vigil on Thursday were Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop.
Panas Gurkha Restaurant, where the vigil took place, has been raising money to help with the rescue efforts in Nepal.
Asked about the importance of the vigil and fundraising, the restaurant’s owner Sujan Katuwal told PA: “It is very, very important.
“At the moment we don’t know how much is damaged.
“It’s a long-term project. Yes, money is there. It might not be enough.
“You know, those farms, those land, all the sand, rocks, and how many years will it take to get rid of those things?”
He added: “I mean we all have seen the pictures, you know, it’s like a movie.
“It did not even have a second for those people, you know, no alarm, nothing.
“And they lost their lives, so many people are missing, so many people have lost their livelihood.”

title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: Curtis Colter Announces Book "A Treasury Of Sale Creek Stories"
all_text:
Coming soon! A Treasury of Sale Creek Stories about Sale Creek people, places, and events will be released on September 27. A book signing will be held that day in the fellowship hall of the Sale Creek Independent Presbyterian Church from 2-5 p.m. for anyone who wishes to purchase a copy locally. Everyone is invited to attend. This will be a come-and-go event.
						The book contains 180 pages and 82 pictures, maps, and illustrations. To purchase a copy online, you may pre-order at coulterpublications.com. The cost is $30.00. Pre-orders will be shipped on September 28.
						Over the past 37 years, I've documented many events from the community’s past, including (1) the great peach and strawberry businesses of the early 1900s, (2) a collection of folklore about the elusive Pitty Pat that haunts Pitty Pat Hollow, (3) stories about WWII veterans, (4) the Welsh coal mining venture of 1868-1913, including the U.S. Soil Conservation Service project to seal the open mine entrances and air shafts in 1994, (5) the 1945 German prisoner-of-war camp, (6) the Civilian Conservation Corps encampment of 1935-1937, (7) the mail and passenger train era from 1880 to 1971, (8) the 1954 plane crash on Sale Creek Mountain that killed six people, and (9) reportedly paranormal encounters in 2004 and 2009 in Burton Hollow, as reported by deer hunters and campers, including two large metropolitan city fire chiefs, their wives, a British stone mason, and a Cleveland, Tn., pastor.
These were major events in the community’s past that needed to be recorded for history. But many more stories needed to be told, which is why this volume exists. I hadn't planned to write another book at first, but after encouragement from my sister and brother-in-law, Elaine and Carey Jackson, I decided to write one more. A Treasury of Sale Creek Stories is a collection of 50 stories about Sale Creek people, places, and events, including one about a friendly old black dog that wandered into the community, adopted several families, and began attending church services with a group of children. I shared some of these stories on my Facebook page, but I haven't published the rest.
Some of the stories come from my earlier books. I included them in this volume because those books have been out of print for over 35 years, and I wanted new, younger readers to have a chance to read them.
						The book contains 14 World War II stories, including one about a Sale Creek farm boy who trained as a cook in the Army and was sent to England. One day, he was asked to prepare lunch for King George VI of England and his entourage. Another story recounts an Army training plane that made an emergency landing in a farmer’s wheat field along Dayton Pike, causing a three-day stir.
						Four tributes honor notable individuals, including a local handyman known only as Wilbur; a distinguished and memorable school principal, William G. Eldridge; a revered music teacher, Ernestine Eldridge; and a Sale Creek native, decorated World War II veteran, and well-known vocational agriculture and mathematics teacher, Merle Crawley.
						The story of Charles (Ches) McCartney, the famous Goat Man of Jeffersonville, Ga., is also included. McCartney brought his traveling train wreck through Sale Creek several times, with the wagon pulled by a herd of up to 30 goats.
						Geographical features are also covered. How did some of the roads in Sale Creek get their names? What is Tater Knob? What is the story behind the Coulterville Lagoon? Where was the Patterson Spring, and what happened to it? All these accounts are included.
						“The Mill Dam – A Sale Creek Icon” recounts the Mill Dam’s history from its construction in 1820 to its destruction by a flood in the 1930s. From a swimming area to a fishing hole to a picnic spot, and even its haunting by the Pitty Pat, the Mill Dam has been part of Sale Creek lore for more than 200 years.
						Perry Mason never had a case like this one – “The Case of the Janitor Running the School!” This is no joke. In 1916, the principal of Sale Creek High School was accused of being unable to make a school decision without conferring with his janitor in the boiler room. Find out why this accusation was made. The controversy eventually boiled over (pun intended), leading to a heated (another pun) meeting between the superintendent and 17 irate, influential Sale Creek residents, who demanded that the janitor be fired and the principal be ousted. To learn how the case turned out, buy the book!
						I retell the story of the Civilian Conservation Corps Camp from 1935 to 1937 from my 1990 book, A Sentimental Journey Down Country Roads. The CCC boys carried out conservation projects to control flooding, prevent soil erosion, and fight forest fires.
						The saga of the taverns and roadhouses that lined Dayton Pike from Sale Creek to the county line in the 1930s and 1940s is recounted in “What was the Dead Rat?” The narrative explains why the Rat was notorious, as it was probably one of the most violent honky-tonks in the area at that time. At least four killings occurred at the infamous roadhouse.
						The story of the little-known Black community in Coulterville is included, based on information from 1990 interviews with former Coulterville residents who remembered many of the families who lived there. All those families moved out of Coulterville before 1950. The Salvation of Bob Martin tells the story of a small, 23-year-old man who had to defend himself against an oversized town bully on Christmas night in 1927. The brawl left the bully with fatal injuries and the defender facing murder charges.
						The story of eleven-year-old Milford Guy is one of tragedy and courage. In 1938, while playing at a friend’s house, he was accidentally shot and paralyzed. His courage and resilience in facing his disability during the remaining five years of his life inspired many people in Sale Creek and at Erlanger Hospital during his intermittent hospital stays. Even President Franklin Roosevelt learned of his condition and helped secure medical care for Milford that his parents could not afford. Milford died in 1943, three weeks before his sixteenth birthday. His courage and resilience inspired everyone who knew him.
						The stories of nine train wrecks are told, including a 1909 crash that killed three people and injured ten more at Retro (current-day Bakewell) in ‘Possum Creek Gulch. Another little-known story is a 1937 head-on collision of two trains in the Ragan Hill Cut, which killed three more train crewmen. In addition to those two wrecks, seven more rail accidents are mentioned, including four at Coulterville (one a head-on collision in 1902) and three more at Sale Creek. One involved several boxcars loaded with cases of beer that derailed north of the Rock Creek trestle, slid down an embankment, and burst open, spilling beer into the woods and down the embankment. The wreck drew an army of drunks, layabouts, lazy bones, and town ne’er-do-wells who enthusiastically helped the railroad company clean up the mess in a finders-keepers operation.
						Three stories about hobos are told, including one titled “Chauncey Reavley and James Kill Bedbugs,” about two desperate, hungry Sale Creek kings of the road who hoodwinked an entire Indiana town into buying ground-up brick dust they advertised as bed bug powder. Their scam generated enough money to buy food for their trip home.
						An 1869 shootout titled “Shootout at the Beene House” involved ten people at the home of a local teacher. When the smoke of battle cleared that day, two people lay dead on the floor, and five more were wounded, two critically, in a blazing gunfight that matched the violence of the shootout at the OK Corral. The story is recounted through testimony from a descendant of one of the shooters and through newspaper articles that offered additional details.
						An historically significant yet little-known event occurred on April 30, 1909 – an outbreak of 43 tornadoes across the Southeastern United States, including one that ravaged Coulterville, damaging or destroying two schools, completely destroying the Sale Creek Cumberland Presbyterian Church, uprooting trees and twisting them off at their bases, and leveling houses, barns, groves of fruit trees, and outbuildings.
						The book includes stories about three forgotten cemeteries in Coulterville, along with details about some of the people buried there. The forgotten cemeteries are the Pat Thomas, Martin, and Miller-Nelson Cemeteries. It also features stories from three other major cemeteries: Patterson, McDonald, and Welsh-Rogers.
						Lastly, the story of three Confederate soldiers’ graves found in a resident’s yard near Mill Dam Bridge in August 2025 is told, including how they were discovered. Those graves date to the Battle of Chickamauga in September 1863. These stories are uniquely Sale Creek. Anyone interested in this town’s history or stories from small-town America will find this book entertaining and informative.

title: Delivering aid to Nepal flood survivors 'very, very difficult': UN
all_text:
Delivering aid to Nepal flood survivors 'very, very difficult': UN
Communities near the epicentre of the catastrophic glacial mountain collapse in Nepal remain cut off, with destroyed roads, bridges and hydropower dams.
People salvage usable materials from their houses deluged in sludge following flash floods at Trishuli Center in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Sep 3, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Arun Sankar)
KATHMANDU: The United Nations warned on Thursday (Sep 3) of the immense challenge of reaching Nepal flood survivors, with destroyed roads forcing aid workers to consider using cargo drones and porters to reach isolated Himalayan communities.
More than 1,200 people have been killed, and some 5,600 are missing on both sides of the China-Nepal border since the catastrophic glacial mountain collapse on Aug 26, according to tolls by both nations on Thursday.
"It is just incredible - the magnitude of the disaster, the magnitude of the destruction," UN Resident Coordinator Lila Pieters Yahia told reporters in Kathmandu.
More than 800 foreigners from at least 34 countries are among those missing, including tourists and pilgrims, in both Nepal and Tibet in China.
In Kathmandu, families of some of the missing foreigners said they were combing hospitals and morgues for any information.
"I feel desperate, it's been so many days," said 53-year-old US citizen Sanjeev Rai, who flew to Nepal to look for his wife, one of around 75 Americans missing.
In China, photographs of missing people are being shared on social media by relatives hoping for news.
"Hurry up and come back, your parents miss you a lot, we need you," one woman wrote on a popular platform, posting an image of her relative, a police officer, and his wife.
Beijing keeps tight control over media access and information, and foreign journalists are restricted from reporting in Tibet.
"VERY, VERY DIFFICULT"
Floods tore through mountain districts, destroying roads, bridges and hydropower dams.
Communities near the epicentre remain cut off, with the UN working alongside Nepal's government to get emergency supplies into devastated areas.
"Access has been very, very, very difficult," Pieters Yahia said, noting that UN agencies had delivered water and and sanitation kits, as well as food and medicine.
"Those are the most essential, particularly for the people who are in the epicentre."
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, in a briefing to diplomats in Kathmandu on Thursday, called it a "Himalayan tsunami".
"I can say from first-hand observation that the reality on the ground is far more severe than images can convey," he said. "This is not an ordinary flood".
Foreign ministry spokesman Lok Bahadur Poudel Chhetri said Nepal needed specialised international assistance, including heavy-lift drones and temporary bridges, as well as body bags and DNA testing kits to help identify the dead.
He said Nepal also needed a mobile air traffic control system and broadband seismometers to monitor ground vibrations.
More than 21,000 Nepali security personnel are working on search, rescue and relief operations.
Nepali rescuers, aided by experts from India, China and South Korea, continue searching for survivors feared trapped inside hydropower tunnels, but teams have repeatedly hit dead ends, and no one has been confirmed alive.
The energy ministry said a committee will be set up to coordinate with rescuers and provide necessary assistance to the families of missing hydropower workers.
At a relief camp in Nepal's Nuwakot district, an AFP journalist saw flood survivors waiting for their names to be called before collecting bags of rice, instant noodles, cooking oil and biscuits.
Pieters Yahia said the UN was discussing with the government "how to use helicopters and cargo drones to be able to deliver aid".
MONITORING AND DATA SHARING
The UN may also turn to Nepal's porters, accustomed to carrying heavy loads through some of the world's toughest mountain terrain during trekking and climbing expeditions, to "bring the aid as soon as possible", the resident coordinator said.
Pieters Yahia warned that gaps in assistance were inevitable given the scale of the catastrophe.
"The magnitude of the disaster is so big that there will always be gaps," she said.
Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China's account of the disaster, but Beijing insists that the "release of information has been open, transparent and timely".
The disaster highlights the need for better long-term monitoring, data sharing and coordination across the Himalayas, experts say.
"What we really need is a dedicated mechanism ... which works around the clock," Saswata Sanyal with the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development told AFP.
Nepal's disaster authority said Thursday that the number of bodies recovered was 1,259, with 5,083 people missing - a sharp rise from the previous figure issued earlier in the day.
In China, state media say 21 people had been killed, and 541 people are missing.
That takes the overall toll to 1,280 people, with 5,624 missing.

title: Joanna Lumley says ‘heartbreaking’ Nepal flood could have been predicted
all_text:
Dame Joanna Lumley has said the “heartbreaking” flash flood in Nepal “could have maybe been predicted” as she attended a vigil to remember those affected by the disaster.
The 80-year-old actress, who has visited Nepal on numerous occasions and has strong ties with the Gurkha community, told the Press Association seeing the flood sweep through the northern part of the country last week “broke her heart”.
Dame Joanna joined members of London’s Nepalese community at a candlelit vigil at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath, south-east London, on Thursday afternoon.
Around fifty people came together at the restaurant to pray for the communities affected by the catastrophe, observe a minute of silence and light candles.
Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday said 1,252 deaths had been recorded since the flash flood on August 26.
It added around 4,200 people remained missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 34 countries.
On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people are currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.
During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: “I think, actually, in this country and around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.
“The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.
“These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn’t something that we haven’t heard of and thought of before.
“When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers.”
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and China.
It added that a “glacial collapse and debris flow” caused “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream”.
Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.
Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, “it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around”.
“It seems that we have been warned about this over the years,” she added.
“Now, there are two camps, as we both know: there is the people who believe that climate change is largely affected by mankind and those who just say that it’s completely a natural phenomenon.
“I belong to the first camp, which is that I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.
“And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there.”
Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.
Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.
Also present at the vigil on Thursday were Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop.
Panas Gurkha Restaurant, where the vigil took place, has been raising money to help with the rescue efforts in Nepal.
Asked about the importance of the vigil and fundraising, the restaurant’s owner Sujan Katuwal told PA: “It is very, very important.
“At the moment we don’t know how much is damaged.
“It’s a long-term project. Yes, money is there. It might not be enough.
“You know, those farms, those land, all the sand, rocks, and how many years will it take to get rid of those things?”
He added: “I mean we all have seen the pictures, you know, it’s like a movie.
“It did not even have a second for those people, you know, no alarm, nothing.
“And they lost their lives, so many people are missing, so many people have lost their livelihood.”

title: Delaware County Acquires 70 Flood Gauges to Track Water Levels in Real Time
all_text:
Delaware County Acquires 70 Flood Gauges to Track Water Levels in Real Time
Delaware County is installing 70 AWARE flood gauges to monitor water levels in real time, report data online, and support emergency response and future planning needs. The project responds to…
Delaware County is installing 70 AWARE flood gauges to monitor water levels in real time, report data online, and support emergency response and future planning needs.
The project responds to increasing flood risk from more frequent and intense rainfall. The gauges aim to improve data-driven decision-making for infrastructure resilience, emergency response, and long-term planning.
Flooding is of particular concern in Delco, where much of the land is low-lying and close to the Delaware River and its tributaries.
According to The Philadelphia Inquirer, Philadelphia installed a similar flood monitoring system earlier this year. The city installed flood sensors and cameras in nine locations, including Cobbs Creek, Darby Creek, and the Manayunk Canal. Residents can view flood monitoring data on a live portal.
The Delaware County gauges will be installed at county-owned sites first, such as bridges and parks. Plans call for expanding the gauges to state, PennDOT, and municipal sites under a broader Act 167 stormwater management plan.
According to the county's draft Act 167 plan, potential locations identified in the draft plan include Smedley Park, Catania County Park along Little Crum Creek, Sun Village Park, Clayton County Park, and several county-owned bridges.
The county has identified 230 flood-prone areas and prioritized 130 locations for gauge placement. According to the Inquirer, these locations include the intersection of 69th Street and Marshall Road in Upper Darby, Brookhaven Memorial Park, and the section of Baltimore Pike that crosses Brandywine Creek at the border of Chester County.
Funding for the project comes from a HUD Community Development Block Grant of $107,845 and $224,274 in Pennsylvania Local Share Account grants, with approximately $95,000 of the first round covered by the county's capital budget.

title: Historic church in Asheville works to rebuild after Helene
all_text:
Historic church in Asheville works to rebuild after Helene
ASHEVILLE, N.C. (WLOS) — Nearly two years after Helene devastated western North Carolina, the Cathedral of All Souls in Asheville's Biltmore Village remains a powerful reminder of both the storm's destruction and the community's determination to rebuild.
The historic church was inundated when Helene struck the region on Sept. 27, 2024. Floodwaters pushed through the church's doors and rose from the basement into the nave, damaging much of the building.
Rev. Sarah Hurlburt remembers seeing the force of the flooding as she approached the church that morning.
“As we were standing at that intersection, we looked, and a construction-size dumpster was rushing by through the intersection,” Hurlburt recalled. “It was terrifying.”
Inside the sanctuary, the rising water tossed the church’s massive solid-oak pews around the room, she says, like “tinker toys.”
All Souls had survived major floods in 1916 and 2004, but Helene was different.
“This flood was so big and so devastating that we could not help anybody,” Hurlburt said, “because we were completely inundated.”
Today, the church remains fenced off as restoration work continues. Brick walkways were warped by water, herringbone floors buckled, and the building’s electrical and air-conditioning systems were destroyed.
Its congregation, however, is undaunted.
“We’re going to do everything we can to upgrade every space for resiliency, to keep this beauty, to protect it and to make it last for generations to come,” Hurlburt said.
The Cathedral of All Souls was built by George Vanderbilt using the same architect, Richard Hunt, who designed the Biltmore House. The church opened its doors on Christmas Eve, 1895, welcoming all through its doors.
In the 1980s, All Souls became the first church in North Carolina to include an LGBTQ Christian ministry. Over the years, the church acquired an affectionate nickname: “All Sorts.”
“Yes, we are All Souls — and we are All Sorts, as well,” Hurlburt said. “And that’s the goal.”
Now, the congregation is asking the wider community to help bring All Souls back to life. A 100-foot “Putt Challenge” is planned for Sept. 15 outside the Biltmore Village church to raise money for the restoration. The event will bring together food, music and golf, with proceeds benefiting the effort to restore the Cathedral of All Souls.
For a church that has endured more than a century of change — and now one of the region’s most devastating storms — the goal remains the same: to reopen its doors and continue serving the community for generations to come.

title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.

title: Toronto storm cleanup begins as thousands remain without power across Ontario
all_text:
Toronto storm cleanup begins as thousands remain without power across Ontario
Toronto Hydro reported about 8,300 homes and businesses without electricity early Thursday
Thousands of people remained without power across Toronto and southern Ontario on Thursday after a severe storm brought torrential rain, flooding, hail and widespread damage.
Toronto Hydro reported about 8,300 homes and businesses without electricity early Thursday, while Hydro One said more than 47,000 customers remained offline across the province.
Flooding forced closures on major Toronto roads, including parts of Yonge Street and the Don Valley Parkway, while some subway services were disrupted during Wednesday's evening rush hour.
Toronto officials said the city received roughly 1,000 service requests following the storm.
“City crews have been clearing debris and sediment and sweeping roadways since flood waters began receding overnight,” the city said on its website.
Officials said closures would remain until cleanup was completed and roads were considered safe.
The storm brought large hail and raised concerns about possible tornado activity.
Toronto Pearson Airport received about 40 millimetres of rain, leading to flight delays and cancellations.
The airport said operations were “returning to normal” Thursday morning but advised passengers to check their flight status.
The storm also caused significant damage to Toronto's 50,000-capacity Rogers Stadium.

title: Hikers describe intense rain and wind before floodwaters ravage Grand Canyon
all_text:
Like clockwork, clouds build up in the afternoon, the wind starts to swirl and the skies darken. Then the rain comes.
Sometimes it is just a few drops. But on this August afternoon, the monsoon kicked into high gear, setting its sights on a remote section of the Grand Canyon's North Rim. Down below, dozens of hikers were setting up camp along Bright Angel Creek and admiring the towering walls they eventually would have to traverse on the way back up.
Recommended Videos
It wasn't long before muddy water came rushing down the creek. The sound was deafening as it crashed against the rocks, carrying with it tree branches, sediment and other debris.
Violent thunderstorms and subsequent flash flooding are nothing new during the summer months in the southwestern United States. Those in the canyon last Saturday knew the risks, but this storm packed an extra punch, washing out key footbridges and doing more damage to infrastructure than previous decades of turbulent water.
Two people died and at least one is still missing. More than 80 people were airlifted out of the canyon, and the National Park Service is assessing the damage.
Forecasts warned of severe storms and flood risks
A storm of generational proportions — that is how some of the hikers described it in interviews with The Associated Press. Some talked about scrambling to higher ground as the rushing water approached. Others hunkered down under a ledge to avoid falling rocks.
“It was for sure some of the worst acute fast-forming weather I have ever seen in my time, whether it’s in the mountains or marine environments or in the desert Southwest,” said Drew Harrell, an emergency medicine physician with University of New Mexico Hospital who was on a training mission at the time as medical director for Grand Canyon National Park.
Harrell is no stranger to working in austere environments and has hiked rim-to-rim more than a dozen times. He and his team had checked the weather before starting their annual trip. They were more worried about afternoon temperatures stretching into the triple digits rather than rain.
But this storm, Harrell said, seemed to come out of the blue just as his six-member group entered “The Box,” the final 3 miles (4.8 kilometers) before Phantom Ranch, an oasis at the bottom of the Grand Canyon.
“It went from relatively clear skies to blowing winds in the time frame of about a minute,” he said, estimating the gusts at 40 mph (64 kph).
Hikers had little time to act
Within minutes, torrential rains, gusting winds and even hail enveloped hikers along the creek.
“We were concerned that there would be rocks and just flooding coming down from both sides of the canyon on top of us,” said Parth Desai, another physician who was with the group.
As emergency room doctors do, they weighed their options and calculated the risks as conditions changed around them.
“We saw basically the flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” Desai said. “And then we were concerned about a lightning strike.”
They made another run for it, heading down the trail toward Phantom Ranch. They maneuvered around cottonwood trees brought down by the first microburst when they saw more debris rushing toward them. They scrambled through cactus to reach higher ground.
Floodwaters overtake what is usually a shady oasis
Up the creek at the Cottonwood Campground, Mike Sumaruk and his friend were relaxing after a nearly 7-mile (11-kilometer) hike down into the canyon. The wind started howling, and the rain intensified.
“I jumped into my tent because I thought it was going to blow away and was trying to hold it down,” he said in a phone interview Tuesday.
Then he heard this roar.
“I thought it was like thunder in the distance, but it wasn’t going away. And I said, that’s not thunder, and I unzipped the tent and got out and saw the huge wall of water,” Sumaruk said. “We just left everything.”
The Tulsa, Oklahoma, resident has hiked plenty of mountain peaks over the years, but this was his first time in the Grand Canyon. It was gorgeous, he said, lamenting that he wasn't able to see more of the natural wonder.
Sumaruk used an emergency phone at an unstaffed ranger station to contact park authorities, telling them he and about a dozen others were stranded. A park ranger traveling on foot eventually reached the group, and they waited until Sunday to be airlifted to the South Rim, where the Red Cross was waiting and counselors were on hand to help.
Harrell shared Sumaruk's appreciation for the park staff, particularly the rangers down in the canyon. He credited them with moving dozens of people at Phantom Ranch to safer areas before water took out the bridges.
“They mitigated the opportunity for there to have been more serious loss of life or injuries,” Harrell said.
The trail turned into a river
Tom Monroe and two friends set out early Saturday from the North Rim. Knowing it was monsoon season, and after seeing light rain the day before, they tried to keep an eye on the weather — though scant cellphone reception made that difficult.
Monroe said they decided to proceed after one hiker they met told them the forecast looked mild. Another who had just climbed the trail reported the way was clear.
They were aiming for Cottonwood Campground. In the first mile, it started sprinkling.
“Then it started just opening up, holy hell raining on us,” said Monroe, 59, of Flagstaff, Arizona, who runs a business making custom food-storage bags for campers.
The trio kept going, figuring it would let up. The downpour continued, mixed with thunder and lightning. Runoff started funneling down the trail. It looked almost like a river, Monroe said.
One friend took shelter in a small alcove in the canyon wall. Monroe huddled under an overhang that protected him — not just from the water but also from sand, mud and rocks falling with it.
“On either side you could see rocks the size of footballs or beach balls coming down the cliffs from the top,” he said.
The friend who was farther ahead had to scramble up a steep slope, where he grabbed tree roots to keep from getting swept away.
The 20-minute downpour seemed to last forever, Monroe said.
“None of us can really stop thinking about it,” Monroe said in a phone interview Wednesday, safely back home in Flagstaff.
Flooding doesn't dampen hikers' outdoor plans
Monroe and his friends already were planning to head outdoors again this weekend, just staying a little closer to home and doing some car camping.
And Sumaruk is thinking about a return trip to the Grand Canyon whenever hikers are allowed again. He will be watching and waiting as the National Park Service begins the arduous process of rebuilding a key water-supply line that was severely damaged, fixing the miles of trail that were washed out and replacing the footbridges.
He said he understands “weather happens” and it will take time for the canyon to recover. Years of research went into his first trip along with months of planning and training, and he is not giving up.
“I'm definitely going to give it another shot,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, and Jamie Stengle in Dallas, contributed to this report. Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Bloomington Police respond to community inquiries regarding unannounced federal immigration operations | WBIW
all_text:
BLOOMINGTON — Addressing a flood of inquiries from concerned residents, the Bloomington Police Department (BPD) issued a statement clarifying that local law enforcement was not notified of—and did not assist with—recent activity conducted by federal immigration authorities in Bloomington and Monroe County.
The department’s response follows reports and social media documentation of federal operations occurring across the area, including detentions near local commercial areas and traffic stops.
Local Police Clarify Autonomy and Lack of Advance Notice
BPD confirmed that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) provided no advance notice regarding planned enforcement actions, nor did federal agencies share information regarding the number of individuals detained or arrested in the city.
| Key Fact | Department Clarification |
| Federal Advance Notice | None provided; federal agencies are not legally required to notify local police. |
| BPD Participation | Zero; BPD officers have not assisted federal agents with any detainments. |
| Detainee Status & Location | Unknown; local police do not have access to transfer or detention destination details. |
“We understand the concerns being expressed by community members and the desire to get answers to questions,” BPD said in a public statement.
Federal Contact Information Provided for Public Inquiries
To assist community members seeking information regarding recent operations or attempting to locate family members, BPD contacted the Department of Homeland Security directly to obtain official inquiry channels.
Residents seeking verified information about federal immigration activity in Monroe County are instructed to contact DHS using the following numbers:
- Public Information Officer: 312-260-9513
- ICE Detainment Information Hotline: 872-351-3990
Unannounced Federal Presence Triggers Community Response
Under federal law, agencies operating under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security—including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)—maintain independent jurisdiction and operate without obligation to coordinate with or notify municipal police departments.
The unannounced operations led to widespread unease throughout the Bloomington area, prompting temporary precautionary closures of several local businesses and inquiries to municipal offices. BPD urges community members to reach out directly to the federal contacts provided above for all official status updates regarding federal immigration actions.

title: Inside the failed mission to eliminate FEMA
all_text:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency is no longer in the Trump administration's crosshairs, according to its former leader.
President Trump has made no secret of his disdain for the country's top disaster agency. In the first week of his second term, he attacked FEMA, saying, "I think, frankly, FEMA is not good," arguing that the agency should be eliminated. That rhetoric was echoed by top administration officials, including then-Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, who controlled the agency's budget.
Other federal agencies have since been stripped down or even eliminated, including the Department of Education, Voice of America and USAID.
But despite his own significant efforts to dismantle FEMA, the man who ran the agency at the time says FEMA isn't going anywhere.
"I think they're probably in a go-along-to-get-along kind of mode," says David Richardson, who led FEMA as acting administrator for much of 2025 and has since left the federal government. "I don't see there being a whole lot of change."
That shift is apparent inside the agency. In recent months, the fear of wholesale agency abolition or mass layoffs has dissipated among FEMA workers, according to multiple current FEMA employees who requested anonymity because they fear retaliation for speaking to a journalist. But the attempts to kill it have compounded some of FEMA's longstanding problems, like understaffing and delays in getting disaster recovery money to survivors.
"Looking back, I think what we saw was an ill-advised attempt to reduce the size of FEMA without fully understanding all the different functions that the agency has," says Andrew Rumbach, who studies disaster policy at the nonprofit Urban Institute.
A recent report from the Government Accountability Office raised concerns about whether the agency is adequately staffed. Parts of the agency that handle disaster recovery are still understaffed and struggling to get long-delayed money to disaster-stricken states, according to the FEMA employees who spoke to NPR.
It's only now that "serious reform efforts" are potentially on the horizon for the agency, Rumbach says, and those efforts no longer include eliminating it.
In response to questions from NPR about whether the agency's goals have changed since the president took office, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email, "FEMA remains fully operational and focused on its core mission of helping people before, during, and after disasters. As a matter of policy, we do not comment on accounts in forthcoming books, internal operational deliberations, or personnel matters." The White House declined to comment.
An inside account of the mission to eliminate FEMA
In one of his first interviews since leaving the agency late last year, Richardson sat down with NPR to talk about his time at FEMA and what he saw as his mission while he was there.
Richardson, who served as an artillery officer in the U.S. Marines for more than 20 years, arrived in FEMA's top job "reluctantly" and with no experience with disaster management. "FEMA's not my thing," he says.
Still, he says he was ready to take on the job because he had previously led efforts to cut the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction office within DHS.
"There was resentment towards FEMA. The president's intent was to shut it down or drastically reform it, and my predecessor wasn't moving fast enough in that direction," he says. "I went there for three things: to get FEMA through hurricane season, either shut it down or drastically reduce its size, and get it ready for rebranding."
Richardson says he arrived at FEMA in May 2025 with a plan to cut the number of employees at FEMA headquarters from about 6,000 to no more than 2,000 by November 2025.
"I always think that you can do more with less people, to a degree. At some point it's self-defeating. But it's definitely self-defeating to have too many people," says Richardson. "I'm a small-government person."
Deanne Criswell, who ran FEMA for four years under the Biden administration, says Richardson's description of FEMA as bloated and in need of drastic cuts suggests he does not understand the agency he briefly ran. She agrees that there are personnel changes that could make FEMA more efficient and effective, but "you can't just indiscriminately cut," she says. "It's only going to hurt the person who has the most need after a disaster."
The Trump administration's approach to cutting FEMA's spending and staffing has also struggled in the face of court challenges. An early attempt by the Trump administration to end a major grant program for disaster preparedness failed after a court challenge, and temporary workers who were terminated earlier this year are suing the agency. This summer, FEMA started rehiring many of those who were terminated.
"Dave, things have changed"
Within months of taking over the agency, Richardson realized that, as he puts it, "the focus was quickly shifting."
He says DHS leadership did not approve a plan he shared to downsize FEMA starting at the end of October 2025, one month before the end of the Atlantic hurricane season. Meanwhile, the president appointed a council of emergency experts to make recommendations about how to reform the agency, and Richardson says he started to wonder if the administration's goals had changed.
In July 2025, he says, he got his answer. As he recounts in a new book, Texas Flood: Power, Money, Politics, History, Bureaucracy and Tragedy, a DHS deputy chief of staff told him, "Dave, things have changed," before explaining that the president's council, not Richardson, would decide the future of FEMA.
Indeed, at public meetings of the council that summer, members discussed a variety of recommendations for whether and how to cut FEMA's workforce. At those meetings, emergency managers from powerful states led by Republican governors, including Texas and Florida, discussed the importance of reforming FEMA, but did not publicly advocate for eliminating it.
"I think that's where we started to see the rhetoric start to change about FEMA," says Criswell. "There are so many communities, and many Republican communities, that depend on the aid that you couldn't just get rid of it without having a negative impact."
The politics began to look more complicated, says Richardson. He writes that he supported the work of the council and continued to advocate for major cuts to FEMA, but "over the next few months, each time I received a call from DHS HQ complaining about the size of FEMA, I reminded them I could cut the size of the agency's HQ in half the next day; I only needed the green light."
Richardson says he never got the green light to make major cuts to FEMA staff.
New leadership and new reforms
Richardson resigned from FEMA in late 2025, and Noem was fired in March of this year.
Noem's replacement at DHS, Markwayne Mullin, was previously a senator from Oklahoma and has extensive experience working with FEMA after major disasters in the state, Rumbach points out. Last month, the Senate confirmed Cameron Hamilton to lead FEMA. Hamilton had previously served as the agency's acting administrator before Richardson took over, but Richardson felt he "wasn't moving fast enough."
In his introductory email to FEMA staff, obtained by NPR, Hamilton wrote that he looks forward to "strengthening the agency for the future."
Meanwhile, the president's FEMA Review Council submitted its recommendations earlier this year and called for states to take more responsibility for disasters. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Hamilton promised to come up with a plan to implement some of those recommendations. Just this week, the agency announced a pilot program with the state of Indiana aimed at getting disaster relief money to the state more quickly for flood repairs.
Rumbach says that approach is very different from Richardson's. "Those are the kind of improvements I'd hope to see in the coming years," he says. "Compared to some of the more dramatic and draconian cuts that were being recommended."
But many of the most sweeping FEMA reforms, such as making the agency report directly to the president and overhauling the system for getting money to individual disaster survivors, would require the White House and Congress to work together. That doesn't appear to be a priority for the administration today. A bipartisan FEMA reform bill is waiting in committee, and President Trump has rarely spoken about FEMA this summer, even after major disasters, including floods and catastrophic wildfires.
Copyright 2026 NPR

Joanna Lumley says ‘heartbreaking’ Nepal flood could have been predicted
all_text:
Dame Joanna Lumley has said the “heartbreaking” flash flood in Nepal “could have maybe been predicted” as she attended a vigil to remember those affected by the disaster.
The 80-year-old actress, who has visited Nepal on numerous occasions and has strong ties with the Gurkha community, told the Press Association seeing the flood sweep through the northern part of the country last week “broke her heart”.
Dame Joanna joined members of London’s Nepalese community at a candlelit vigil at Panas Gurkha Restaurant in Blackheath, south-east London, on Thursday afternoon.
Around fifty people came together at the restaurant to pray for the communities affected by the catastrophe, observe a minute of silence and light candles.
Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday said 1,252 deaths had been recorded since the flash flood on August 26.
It added around 4,200 people remained missing, including 590 foreign nationals from 34 countries.
On Tuesday, Foreign Office minister Lord Wood of Anfield told the House of Lords that 36 British people are currently unaccounted for, up from the previous total of 33.
During the vigil, Dame Joanna said: “I think, actually, in this country and around the world our hearts have been absolutely broken by what happened in Nepal.
“The sense that it could have maybe been predicted by all the people who understood that by human activities somehow the world seems to be changing, seems to be getting warmer.
“These catastrophes, the great Himalayan glaciers melting, isn’t something that we haven’t heard of and thought of before.
“When you see the catastrophic outcome, I think we feel completely hopeless every day we look in the papers.”
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event occurred near the border between Nepal and China.
It added that a “glacial collapse and debris flow” caused “subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream”.
Rescue efforts had previously been hampered by fears of more flooding from a lake formed by the glacier collapse which sparked the flooding.
Dame Joanna said having visited and travelled in the country, “it breaks my heart because I know how difficult it is to get around”.
“It seems that we have been warned about this over the years,” she added.
“Now, there are two camps, as we both know: there is the people who believe that climate change is largely affected by mankind and those who just say that it’s completely a natural phenomenon.
“I belong to the first camp, which is that I do believe that what we do here, and the fossil fuels we burn and the plastic waste in the sea and so on, I do believe that is making the world a sicker place and a weaker place.
“And the places which are melting fastest are the high mountains and places, and so the Himalayas are there.”
Dame Joanna is the patron of healthcare charity Doctors for Nepal and vice patron of The Gurkha Welfare Trust, which provides aid to Gurkha veterans who served in the British Army.
Her father served in the 6th Gurkha Rifles, a regiment of the British Indian Army, during the Second World War.
Also present at the vigil on Thursday were Vice Lord-Lieutenant Colonel Jane Davis, former Coronation Street star Sally Lindsay, drummer Steve White and Greenwich mayor David Wardrop.
Panas Gurkha Restaurant, where the vigil took place, has been raising money to help with the rescue efforts in Nepal.
Asked about the importance of the vigil and fundraising, the restaurant’s owner Sujan Katuwal told PA: “It is very, very important.
“At the moment we don’t know how much is damaged.
“It’s a long-term project. Yes, money is there. It might not be enough.
“You know, those farms, those land, all the sand, rocks, and how many years will it take to get rid of those things?”
He added: “I mean we all have seen the pictures, you know, it’s like a movie.
“It did not even have a second for those people, you know, no alarm, nothing.
“And they lost their lives, so many people are missing, so many people have lost their livelihood.”
